<explanation>
Below is a tailored set of instructions for drawing a system‐design (architecture) diagram for the Mobile Next “mobile‐mcp” server. Use these guidelines to capture all essential components, their relationships, and the project’s architectural patterns.

1. Project Type and Purpose
   • This is an open‐source, platform‐agnostic CLI/server (Node.js) that implements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for mobile automation.  
   • It exposes a standard MCP interface (via STDIO) so clients (IDEs or agent frameworks) can drive iOS/Android apps on simulators, emulators, or real devices using native accessibility snapshots or image‐based fallbacks.

2. File‐Structure Analysis
   • Top‐level entries:  
     – server.json, package.json, tsconfig.json, build/config files  
     – src/ directory containing all TypeScript modules  
     – test/ directory with corresponding unit tests  
   • Key modules in src/:  
     – index.ts / mobilecli.ts – application entrypoints & CLI parsing  
     – server.ts – Core MCP server implementation (message routing, request/response lifecycle)  
     – android.ts, ios.ts, iphone‐simulator.ts – platform‐specific drivers/interfaces  
     – webdriver‐agent.ts – iOS WebDriverAgent bridge  
     – robot.ts – coordinate‐based tap simulation  
     – png.ts, image‐utils.ts – image decoding & screenshot analysis  
     – logger.ts – centralized logging utility  

3. Architecture from README
   • The README’s “🏗️ Mobile MCP Architecture” diagram (hosted externally) highlights:  
     – Clients (Agents, LLMs, IDEs) ↔ MCP Server ↔ Device drivers (Android, iOS, Simulator)  
     – Fallback flows: Accessibility Tree vs. Screenshot + Image Analysis  
   • Dependencies & protocols:  
     – STDIO (MCP messages)  
     – ADB (Android Platform Tools)  
     – xcrun / simctl / WebDriverAgent (iOS)  
     – Node.js v22+ runtime  

4. Diagram‐Drawing Instructions
   a. Main Components  
      • Client layer: IDEs or Agent Frameworks (e.g., Claude MCP, OpenAI Agent SDK, etc.)  
      • MCP Server (Node.js)  
        – CLI Parser (mobilecli.ts)  
        – Message Router / MCP Engine (server.ts, index.ts)  
        – Logging (logger.ts)  
      • Device‐Connector Plugins  
        – Android Module (android.ts → uses ADB)  
        – iOS Module (ios.ts → uses WebDriverAgent)  
        – Simulator Module (iphone‐simulator.ts → uses simctl)  
      • Interaction Helpers  
        – Image Processing (png.ts, image‐utils.ts)  
        – Robot / Input Simulator (robot.ts)  
      • External Dependencies  
        – Android SDK / adb  
        – Xcode CLI / simctl / WebDriverAgent  
        – Node.js runtime  

   b. Relationships & Data Flow  
      1. Client sends MCP request over STDIO to MCP Server.  
      2. Server parses request in mobilecli.ts, routes via server.ts to appropriate handler.  
      3. Handler invokes platform module (android.ts / ios.ts / simulator).  
      4. Module either:  
         – Queries native accessibility tree → returns structured snapshot.  
         – Captures screenshot via adb/xcrun/webdriveragent → hands off to png.ts + image‐utils.ts → robot.ts for tap coordinates.  
      5. Module returns action result back through the MCP Engine.  
      6. MCP Engine serializes and writes response to STDIO for the client.  

   c. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
      • Plugin pattern: each platform connector implements the same handler interface.  
      • Layered design: CLI layer → Protocol Engine → Driver layer → OS‐level tools → Hardware/device.  
      • Fallback strategy: prioritizes structured accessibility data; falls back to image‐based analysis only when needed.  
      • Single‐process, event‐driven Node.js application.  

   d. Key Technologies & Libraries  
      • Node.js (v22+) & TypeScript  
      • Model Context Protocol (MCP) over STDIO  
      • Android Platform Tools (adb)  
      • Xcode CLI / simctl, WebDriverAgent  
      • PNG decoding libraries as used in png.ts  

5. Tailoring the Diagram for an Open‐Source Tool
   • Emphasize the core MCP interface as the “contract” between clients and this server.  
   • Show ext-point for adding new platform modules (e.g., future Huawei/Electron connectors).  
   • Highlight fallback mechanisms (tree vs. image) as key functional paths.  

6. Diagram‐Style Guidelines
   • Use clear, concise labels on each box.  
   • Draw directional arrows to show request/response flow:  
     – Clients → MCP Server → Platform Modules → OS Tools → Devices  
     – Responses flow back in reverse.  
   • Color code by layer:  
     – Client tools (blue)  
     – MCP Core (green)  
     – Platform Connectors (orange)  
     – Image/Text Helpers (yellow)  
     – External Dependencies / OS Tools (gray)  
   • Group related modules into swimlanes or containers (e.g., “MCP Server”, “Android Driver”).  

7. Final Tips
   • Capture all TS modules as subcomponents of the MCP Server.  
   • Clearly indicate the two primary interaction modes: “Accessibility Snapshot” vs. “Screenshot + Image Analysis → Robot”.  
   • Annotate any important CLI flags or configuration points (server.json).  
   • Keep the diagram at one glance—use nested boxes or grouping rather than too many disconnected arrows.

By following these steps and guidelines, you’ll produce a comprehensive, accurate architecture diagram that reflects Mobile Next’s design, extensibility, and runtime behavior.
